news_summary: Scientists are uncovering fundamental insights into the origins of the universe by exploring forgotten particles and recreating matter from the Big Bang.
news_summary_fr: Les scientifiques acquièrent des connaissances fondamentales sur les origines de l'univers en étudiant des particules tombées dans l'oubli et en recréant la matière issue du Big Bang.
news_summary_es: Los científicos están descubriendo conocimientos fundamentales sobre los orígenes del universo mediante la exploración de partículas olvidadas y la recreación de la materia del Big Bang.

articles.title: Scientists say a forgotten particle may explain why the universe exists
articles.summary: A mysterious particle overlooked for decades may hold the key to why matter survived the Big Bang, allowing stars, planets, and life to exist. Scientists believe this forgotten neutrino reshaped the early universe and may have left detectable gravitational wave signals that could help unlock the cosmos’s deepest mysteries.
articles.content:
Scientists have proposed a surprising new explanation for why the universe exists, and it centers on a mysterious particle that physicists have largely overlooked for decades. Their theory suggests this forgotten particle may have played a crucial role in shaping the early cosmos and allowing matter to survive after the Big Bang.

The research addresses one of the most fundamental mysteries in physics: why does the universe contain matter instead of nothing at all? Scientists believe matter and antimatter were produced in nearly equal amounts in the early universe. When these opposites encounter one another, they annihilate and release energy. If they had existed in perfectly equal quantities, virtually all matter could have disappeared, leaving no material to form stars, planets, or life.

Now, researchers from the University of Southampton and the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur believe they may have found an important piece of the puzzle. Their explanation involves a little-understood relative of the neutrino, an extremely lightweight particle that rarely interacts with ordinary matter.

A Forgotten Particle With a Powerful Role in the Early Universe

The team focused on a type of particle known as a 'decoupled' heavy neutrino. Unlike ordinary neutrinos, this hypothetical heavier relative has generally been considered too weakly connected to other particles to significantly influence the universe.

However, the researchers found that its unusually long lifetime could have made it far more important than previously thought. According to their calculations, the particle may have survived long enough to temporarily dominate the universe's energy density as the cosmos cooled after the Big Bang.

That brief period of dominance could have altered how the early universe evolved, influencing the conditions that ultimately allowed matter to outnumber antimatter.

Dr. Rishav Roshan of the University of Southampton, an author of the study, explained:

"This decoupled heavy neutrino has long been dismissed as an irrelevant background detail in particle physics.

"However, it decays incredibly slowly. As the cosmos cooled after the Big Bang, the particle lived long enough that it temporarily took over the energy density of the universe and triggered a matter-dominated period."

The findings were published in Physical Review Letters, a scientific journal of the American Physical Society.

How a Heavy Neutrino Could Explain Why Matter Survived

Previous attempts to explain why matter prevailed over antimatter generally left out the decoupled heavy neutrino. Because it interacts so weakly with other particles, scientists assumed it would have little influence on the processes responsible for creating the imbalance.

The new research challenges that assumption. The team found that even a particle with extremely weak interactions could indirectly affect the conditions under which matter gained its crucial advantage.

This imbalance, known as matter and antimatter asymmetry, is essential to understanding our existence. For reasons physicists are still trying to explain, the early universe ended up with slightly more matter than antimatter. That small difference allowed some matter to remain after most particles and their antiparticles annihilated one another.

"The fact that we are here at all proves that an asymmetry between matter and antimatter occurred," added Dr. Roshan.

"The decoupled neutrino shifted the temperature in the early universe at which fundamental particles - like electrons and other leptons - interacted with their anti-particles with the help of Standard Model Higgs boson.

"This temperature acts like a switch that shapes how the matter-antimatter imbalance was built up."

The Higgs boson is a fundamental particle associated with the mechanism that gives many elementary particles their mass. In the researchers' proposed scenario, the heavy neutrino changed the temperature conditions governing important particle interactions involving the Higgs boson.

By shifting when these interactions occurred, the particle could have influenced how the imbalance between matter and antimatter developed. In other words, something long considered insignificant may have helped determine why the universe contains matter at all.

Ancient Gravitational Waves Could Reveal the Answer

The theory could also have important implications for understanding how the universe expanded in its earliest stages.

Study co-author Dr. Sudipta Show of the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur said the findings suggest that the forgotten particle may have dramatically altered the expansion history of the young cosmos.

He added: "It offers us a new explanation for how matter won.

"The dramatic shift in the early expansion of the cosmos leaves distinct but detectable imprints of changes, for example on primordial gravitational waves.

"These gravitational wave signatures open up new avenues for us to unravel the evolution of the early universe after the Big Bang."

Gravitational waves are ripples in the fabric of space and time. Scientists believe processes in the extremely early universe may have generated primordial gravitational waves that carry information about conditions from that distant era.

According to the new theory, the temporary dominance of the heavy neutrino could have left recognizable signatures in those ancient signals. Detecting such patterns could eventually provide a way to investigate whether the proposed particle really influenced the universe's earliest evolution.

For now, the explanation remains theoretical. But it offers physicists a new possibility for solving one of cosmology's deepest mysteries: how matter survived when its encounter with antimatter could have left the universe almost entirely empty.

This represents a meaningful advancement in space science with wide-reaching impact on our understanding of the universe.

articles.personality_title_fr: Une particule oubliée pourrait expliquer pourquoi la matière existe dans l'univers
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les scientifiques se demandent depuis longtemps pourquoi l'univers contient de la matière plutôt que rien. Après le Big Bang, matière et antimatière ont été créées en quantités presque égales et se détruisent lorsqu'elles se rencontrent. Si elles s'étaient parfaitement équilibrées, il n'y aurait ni étoiles, ni planètes, ni vie.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Des chercheurs de l'Université de Southampton et de l'Institut indien de technologie de Kanpur ont étudié une particule rarement prise en compte, appelée neutrino lourd « découplé ». Cette particule vit beaucoup plus longtemps que les autres et aurait pu dominer l'énergie de l'univers un court instant après le Big Bang. Cela aurait pu modifier les conditions du cosmos primitif, aidant la matière à surpasser l'antimatière.

**Impact** – Cette découverte remet en question l'idée que ce neutrino lourd était sans importance. Elle montre que même des particules très faiblement interactives peuvent influencer le développement de l'univers. La théorie prédit aussi des motifs uniques dans les ondes gravitationnelles anciennes — des ondulations dans l'espace-temps — qui pourraient être détectées à l'avenir pour tester cette idée.

**Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques chercheront ces signaux particuliers d'ondes gravitationnelles pour voir s'ils correspondent aux effets prévus par le neutrino lourd. S'ils sont trouvés, cela confirmerait le rôle de cette particule dans la formation de l'univers et expliquerait pourquoi la matière a survécu au Big Bang.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Un neutrino lourd longtemps oublié pourrait avoir aidé la matière à survivre au Big Bang, ouvrant de nouvelles voies pour comprendre les origines de l'univers.
articles.personality_title_es: Una partícula olvidada podría explicar por qué existe la materia en el universo
articles.personality_presentation_es:

Si se hubieran equilibrado perfectamente, no habría estrellas, planetas ni vida.

Esta partícula vive mucho más tiempo que otras y pudo haber dominado la energía del universo por un breve momento después del Big Bang. Esto pudo cambiar las condiciones tempranas del cosmos, ayudando a que la materia superara a la antimateria.

**Impacto** – Este descubrimiento desafía la idea antigua de que este neutrino pesado no era importante. Muestra que incluso partículas con interacciones muy débiles pueden afectar cómo se desarrolló el universo. La teoría también predice patrones únicos en ondas gravitacionales antiguas — ondulaciones en el espacio-tiempo — que podrían medirse en el futuro para probar esta idea.

**Próximos pasos** – Los científicos buscarán estas señales especiales en las ondas gravitacionales para ver si coinciden con los efectos previstos por el neutrino pesado. Si se encuentran, confirmaría el papel de esta partícula en la formación del universo y explicaría por qué la materia sobrevivió al Big Bang.

**Resumen en una frase** – Un neutrino pesado olvidado durante mucho tiempo pudo haber ayudado a la materia a sobrevivir al Big Bang, abriendo nuevas formas de entender los orígenes del universo.

articles.title: Scientists smash oxygen nuclei to recreate matter from the Big Bang
articles.summary: Scientists have recreated a primordial state of matter from the dawn of the universe by colliding oxygen nuclei at nearly the speed of light. The surprising results show that this exotic substance can form in smaller, lower-energy collisions than previously demonstrated, challenging the known boundaries of early-universe physics.
articles.content:
New findings from the STAR experiment at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) suggest that scientists can recreate an extraordinary form of matter from the earliest moments of the universe using surprisingly small atomic collisions. By smashing oxygen nuclei together at nearly the speed of light, researchers have uncovered strong evidence of quark-gluon plasma (QGP), an extremely hot and dense state of matter that existed shortly after the Big Bang.

The findings, published in Physical Review Letters, reveal that high-energy streams of particles lose energy as they travel through the material created by these collisions. This effect, called jet quenching, provides an important clue that quark-gluon plasma has formed.

Scientists have previously observed jet quenching in collisions involving much larger atomic nuclei at RHIC, a U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) Office of Science User Facility that operated at Brookhaven National Laboratory from 2000 until 2026. The same effect has also been detected in oxygen collisions at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC), the European Particle Physics Laboratory.

What makes the new RHIC findings especially significant is that the oxygen collisions occurred at substantially lower energies. The results establish a new lower boundary for the conditions known to produce quark-gluon plasma in this small collision system, helping scientists narrow down what it takes to create matter resembling that of the infant universe.

"The QGP is believed to be the form of matter that filled the early universe -- before the protons and neutrons that make up today's atoms formed. Understanding its properties is essential for uncovering how the early universe evolved in its first microseconds," said Li Yi, a professor of physics at Shandong University who oversaw the STAR analysis.

"One of the most powerful ways scientists study the QGP is by identifying where its signatures appear -- and just as importantly, where these signatures turn off," she said.

Rongrong Ma, a STAR physicist at Brookhaven Lab, explained why investigating smaller collisions is so valuable.

"This analysis is pushing the boundaries to an extreme case to help us learn something about this jet quenching phenomenon and the conditions needed to generate a QGP."

How Scientists Recreate Matter From the Early Universe

RHIC was designed specifically to produce and investigate quark-gluon plasma. Traditionally, researchers have accomplished this by accelerating gold nuclei to enormous speeds and crashing them into one another.

Each gold nucleus contains 79 protons and 118 neutrons. When two such nuclei collide with sufficient energy, the boundaries of their protons and neutrons effectively break down, releasing the quarks and gluons inside them. The tremendous energy of the impact also generates thousands of additional quarks and gluons through the conversion of energy into matter, as described by Einstein's famous equation, E=mc2.

The result is a fleeting droplet of primordial matter. It is smaller than an atomic nucleus and survives for less than a billionth of a billionth of a second. Almost immediately, the quarks and gluons recombine into more familiar particles.

Because this exotic substance disappears so quickly, scientists cannot examine it directly. Instead, they use enormous instruments such as the STAR detector to analyze the particles that emerge from the collision.

One particularly revealing clue comes from particles that escape with less energy than expected. Their reduced energy suggests they interacted with the dense mixture of quarks and gluons before escaping.

Researchers pay special attention to jets, which are narrow sprays of extremely energetic particles. These often originate when a quark or gluon from one nucleus strikes a quark or gluon from another, sending two particle jets traveling in opposite directions.

If these paired jets, known as "di-jets," form near the edge of the collision region, one may have to travel farther through the plasma than the other. Comparing their behavior allows scientists to investigate how the surrounding material drains energy from particles passing through it.

Yi offered a familiar comparison to explain the process.

"You can think of it like shooting a bullet through, say, water," Yi said. "Because of the resistance, the bullet will slow down. It's the same thing with these high-energy particles. When they go through the QGP, they will lose energy."

The Telltale Signs of Quark-Gluon Plasma

For decades, RHIC experiments have provided clear evidence of jet quenching in collisions between gold nuclei. The effect is especially noticeable in jets that travel longer distances through the newly created matter.

Scientists believe these particles lose more energy because they encounter more quarks and gluons before escaping. Jets originating closer to the outer boundary generally pass through less material and experience fewer interactions.

These measurements helped establish that RHIC was successfully producing quark-gluon plasma. Additional evidence came from several other experiments, including an unexpected discovery about how the resulting matter behaves.

Scientists observed that relatively low-energy particles emerging from gold collisions moved collectively, following coordinated patterns. This behavior indicated that the plasma flowed almost like a perfect liquid, with extraordinarily little viscosity or internal resistance.

The discovery was a major surprise when researchers first identified it. Collective flow has since become another important "smoking gun" signature of quark-gluon plasma.

Can Tiny Atomic Collisions Create Primordial Matter?

After establishing these signatures in collisions involving large nuclei, physicists began finding similar collective motion in much smaller systems.

Experiments at the LHC, followed by studies at RHIC, detected collective flow when tiny projectiles such as protons, deuterons, and helium-3 nuclei struck much larger gold or lead nuclei. Researchers at the LHC even observed comparable flow patterns in collisions between individual protons.

These results raised a major question. Did the coordinated particle motion mean that these much smaller collisions were also producing quark-gluon plasma, or could another mechanism explain the observations?

Scientists needed a more definitive sign.

"The next natural question is: Can you see jet quenching, the other key signature that QGP is formed, in these very small collision systems?" asked Brookhaven's Ma. "We haven't seen any unambiguous signal, so it's still kind of under debate in these small systems. We want to search for the smallest system where we can still see an unambiguous jet-quenching signal," he said.

To investigate, researchers turned to collisions between oxygen nuclei.

An oxygen nucleus contains just eight protons and eight neutrons, making it far smaller than the gold nuclei typically used in RHIC experiments. Oxygen nuclei also have a relatively symmetrical, spherical shape, which makes the geometry of their collisions easier to analyze.

"That means we can more easily look for signs of asymmetric quenching of di-jets produced close to the edge of the circular interaction region in head-on collisions," said Maowu Nie, an associate professor at Shandong University who contributed to the research.

The scientists could also examine how the outcome changed depending on whether the oxygen nuclei collided directly or merely grazed one another.

"We can also compare how jets behave in head-on central collisions -- those that produce the most particles and therefore have the highest likelihood of making a QGP -- with collisions where the two oxygen nuclei barely strike each other, which aren't expected to generate a QGP."

Nie explained that these grazing collisions are recognizable because they generate far fewer particles than direct impacts.

Oxygen Collisions Reveal a 20% Suppression

To search for jet quenching, the researchers developed an analysis that identifies concentrated streams of high-energy particles and measures how many emerge above a selected energy threshold.

"Our measurements are essentially counting experiments," said Sijie Zhang, who conducted the research for her master's thesis under Yi and Nie at Shandong University and is now pursuing a Ph.D. at Yale University.

"We have an algorithm that finds the collimated groups of high-energy particles, the jets, and we count how many of these particles above a certain energy threshold come out."

Yang He, a former Ph.D. student at Shandong University who developed the analysis framework and now studies oxygen collisions at the LHC, described how the team used different collision types to identify energy loss.

"We compare what we see in back-to-back jets produced near the edge of the system, and we compare what we see in head-on collisions with the counts in non-central collisions where we don't expect to see quenching."

The team analyzed STAR measurements from oxygen collisions conducted at RHIC in 2021, at a collision energy of 200 billion electron volts (GeV).

The results revealed a 20% suppression of high-energy particles associated with jet quenching.

Although this suppression was smaller than what physicists typically measure in gold collisions, that difference was expected because oxygen collisions generate much smaller systems.

Crucially, the observed effect was still strong enough to provide clear evidence that quark-gluon plasma had formed.

Comparing Big Bang Matter at Different Energies

Oxygen offers scientists another important advantage. Apart from proton-proton collisions, it is the only nuclear species that has been investigated in collisions at both RHIC and the LHC.

That gives researchers an unusual opportunity to make an "apples-to-apples" comparison between two facilities operating at very different collision energies.

The LHC carried out its first oxygen collisions in 2025. According to results reported by CERN, those experiments revealed both collective flow and jet quenching, providing additional indications that quark-gluon plasma can form in relatively small nuclear collisions.

However, the LHC operated at collision energies exceeding 5,000 GeV, far above the 200 GeV used in the RHIC measurements.

"With a higher energy collision, it's more likely to create more and more quarks and gluons and a hotter, denser QGP system," Yi said. "That means the jet quenching signal, if it's there, should be bigger at LHC compared to RHIC."

While higher energies make it easier to create the hot, dense conditions needed for quark-gluon plasma, lower-energy experiments may be more useful for determining precisely when those conditions are no longer sufficient.

By reducing the collision energy and using smaller nuclei, physicists can approach the threshold at which the distinctive signatures of primordial matter disappear.

"We are pushing the boundaries in two ways to explore the minimal conditions for creating a QGP, both in terms of the nucleus size by looking at these small oxygen-oxygen collisions, but also by looking at data from lower collision energies -- and we still see this crucial QGP signature. That's a unique feature of our measurement," Ma said.

New Experiments Could Reveal the Limits of Primordial Matter

Although RHIC has now completed its operations, scientists still have additional oxygen collision data to investigate.

During the collider's final experimental run, researchers collected measurements using both STAR and sPHENIX, RHIC's newest detector. The facility concluded its operations with oxygen collisions recorded by both instruments on February 6, 2026.

These remaining datasets could provide further insights into how small a collision system can become, and how low its energy can fall, before quark-gluon plasma can no longer form.

Understanding those limits may help physicists piece together the behavior of matter during the first microseconds of the universe, when quarks and gluons had not yet combined into the protons and neutrons that make up ordinary atoms today.

The research received financial support from the DOE Office of Science, the U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF), and additional international agencies and organizations identified in the scientific publication.

The researchers also used the Open Science Grid, which receives direct support from NSF, along with computing resources at Brookhaven Lab's Scientific Data and Computing Facilities and the National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center (NERSC), a DOE Office of Science User Facility located at DOE's Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.

articles.personality_title: Scientists recreate early-universe matter using smaller oxygen collisions
articles.personality_presentation:

**What happened** – Researchers at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) smashed oxygen nuclei at nearly the speed of light. They found clear signs of QGP forming in these smaller, lower-energy collisions, shown by a 20% drop in energy of particle jets passing through the plasma. This discovery came from experiments done in 2021 and published recently.

**Impact** – Before, QGP was mostly seen in collisions involving large atoms like gold, at much higher energies. articles.personality_title_fr: Des scientifiques recréent la matière de l’univers primordial avec des collisions d’oxygène plus petites
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les scientifiques étudient le plasma quark-gluon (QGP), une matière très chaude et dense apparue juste après le Big Bang. Ils le créent en faisant entrer en collision des noyaux atomiques à grande vitesse pour comprendre l’évolution de l’univers primordial.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Les chercheurs du collisionneur RHIC ont fait entrer en collision des noyaux d’oxygène à presque la vitesse de la lumière. Ils ont trouvé des preuves claires de formation du QGP dans ces collisions plus petites et à plus basse énergie, avec une baisse de 20 % de l’énergie des jets de particules traversant le plasma. Cette découverte vient d’expériences menées en 2021 et récemment publiées.

**Impact** – Avant, le QGP était surtout observé dans des collisions d’atomes lourds comme l’or, à des énergies beaucoup plus élevées. Le voir dans des collisions d’oxygène plus petites et moins énergétiques montre que cette matière primordiale peut se former dans des conditions moins extrêmes que prévu. Cela aide à mieux comprendre les limites précises de l’apparition de cette matière.

**Prochaine étape** – Même si le RHIC a cessé ses opérations, les scientifiques disposent de plus de données sur les collisions d’oxygène à analyser. De nouvelles études chercheront jusqu’où les collisions peuvent devenir petites ou basses en énergie avant que le QGP ne se forme plus, améliorant la connaissance des premiers instants de l’univers.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Des scientifiques ont recréé une forme clé de la matière de l’univers primordial grâce à des collisions d’oxygène plus petites et moins violentes, élargissant notre compréhension des débuts de l’univers.
articles.personality_title_es: Científicos recrean materia del universo temprano con colisiones más pequeñas de oxígeno
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los científicos estudian el plasma de quarks y gluones (QGP), una materia muy caliente y densa que existió justo después del Big Bang. Lo crean chocando núcleos atómicos a gran velocidad para entender cómo evolucionó el universo temprano.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores en el Colisionador Relativista de Iones Pesados (RHIC) chocaron núcleos de oxígeno casi a la velocidad de la luz. Encontraron señales claras de formación de QGP en estas colisiones más pequeñas y con menor energía, mostrando una reducción del 20 % en la energía de los chorros de partículas que atraviesan el plasma. Este hallazgo proviene de experimentos realizados en 2021 y publicados recientemente.

**Impacto** – Antes, el QGP se observaba principalmente en colisiones con átomos grandes como el oro, y a energías mucho más altas. Encontrarlo en colisiones más pequeñas de oxígeno y a menor energía muestra que esta materia primordial puede formarse en condiciones menos extremas de lo que se pensaba. Esto ayuda a entender mejor los límites exactos en que aparece esta materia.

**Próximo paso** – Aunque RHIC ya cerró, los científicos tienen más datos de colisiones de oxígeno para analizar. Nuevos estudios explorarán qué tan pequeñas o de baja energía pueden ser las colisiones antes de que el QGP deje de formarse, mejorando el conocimiento de los primeros microsegundos del universo.

**Resumen en una frase** – Científicos han recreado una forma clave de la materia del universo temprano usando colisiones más pequeñas y suaves de oxígeno, ampliando nuestra comprensión del origen del universo.
